title: Food Science & Functions: Foundations
welcome_lead: Discover what really happens to food when heat hits it.
meta_desc: GCSE food science foundations: gelatinisation, denaturation, coagulation, aeration.
final_note: Naming the change is the first step to controlling it.

concepts.def: Starch granules swell and thicken hot liquid.
Protein structure unravels through heat or acid.
Denatured proteins join and set firm.
Adding air to mixtures for lightness.
Fat coating flour to give crumbly texture.
Mixing oil and water with an emulsifier.

walkthroughs.body_html: When starch granules are heated in liquid, they absorb water, swell and burst, releasing starch that thickens the liquid. Gelatinisation usually starts around 60 °C and completes near 85 °C. It's how sauces, custards and gravies thicken.

Heat (and acids like lemon juice) unravel protein chains — this is denaturation. The unravelled chains then bond with each other and set, called coagulation. Egg white turning from clear to opaque white as it cooks is the classic example.

Aeration traps air in whisked egg whites or creamed butter and sugar. Shortening happens when fat coats flour, blocking gluten and giving short, crumbly pastry. Emulsification combines oil and water using a stabiliser like egg yolk in mayonnaise.
